# Waves and wave transformation

`waves` | Generation, propagation, and transformation of surface gravity waves.

Subtopics: [Wave generation](waves.generation.md), [Nonlinear wave dynamics](waves.nonlinear.md), [Wave transformation](waves.transformation.md)

Papers: 10. Claims: 1. Equations: 0.

## Synthesis

**Well established.** Surface-gravity waves are generated by forcing such as wind and propagate dispersively; decreasing depth causes shoaling, refraction, nonlinear spectral transfer and ultimately breaking, while abrupt or three-dimensional bathymetry produces diffraction, focusing and wave-driven circulation.

**Governing physics.** Gravity and inertia set dispersion, conservation of wave action governs slowly varying propagation, depth contours refract rays, lateral gradients diffract energy, and nonlinear interactions transfer energy among frequencies. Breaking dissipates energy and radiation-stress gradients force mean water levels and currents.

**Dimensionless parameters.** Controls include relative depth kh, wave steepness H/L, Ursell, Iribarren, Froude and Reynolds numbers, depth and slope ratios, directional and frequency bandwidth, relative bathymetric-feature size, breaking index and normalized energy or power flux.

**Major equations.** Core descriptions include linear dispersion and spectral action balance, mild-slope and parabolic equations, Boussinesq systems for weak dispersion and nonlinearity, nonlinear shallow-water limits, Navier–Stokes free-surface models, and momentum equations forced by wave stresses.

**Typical methods.** Wave research combines buoys, pressure and current sensors, SAR and coastal video, laboratory basins, spectral and bispectral analysis, hindcasts, ray and action-balance models, mild-slope/parabolic solvers, Boussinesq models and phase-resolving CFD.

**Numerical models.** Reviewed examples use shallow-water SAR inversion, MIKE21 SW, phase-averaged reef modeling, stochastic and deterministic Boussinesq models, coupled SWAN–Delft3D, poroelastic seabed response and image-based classifiers.

**Experimental datasets.** Evidence includes seven-sensor SAR validation on the French coast, ten months at Hanalei Bay, a natural barred beach, a rocky-shoal storm deployment, submerged-mound experiments, Santa Catarina hindcasts and coastal-video transformation maps.

**Validated ranges.** Examples span offshore-to-20 m isobath wave-power change, 2–8 m rocky-ridge depths, 2.4–4.0 m storm wave heights, 0.3–0.4 m/s observed wave-driven jets, greater-than-twofold mound amplification and 30% directional steepening differences.

**Recent advances.** Recent advances fuse satellite and video observations with models, resolve complex bathymetry on nested grids, model continuous-spectrum nonlinear shoaling, quantify three-dimensional seabed coupling and translate regional hindcasts into resource and hazard products.

**Disagreements.** Phase-averaged models are efficient but can misrepresent steep-feature breaking and energetic swell transformation; deterministic phase-resolving models retain detail at higher cost, while stochastic closures trade phase information for spectral tractability.

**Limitations.** Uncertain winds and offshore boundaries, sparse directional observations, bathymetric resolution, breaking and bottom-friction closures, nonlinear and three-dimensional effects, image visibility and scale separation limit prediction and transfer.

**Open questions.** Priorities include coupled wave–current transformation, extreme and infragravity dynamics, breaking over complex reefs and structures, remote-sensing fusion, climate trends, uncertainty-aware forecasts and links to sediment, flooding and ecosystems.

**Seminal papers.** Linear dispersion, Snell refraction and shoaling theory established basic transformation; spectral balance, radiation stress, mild-slope equations and Boussinesq theory later connected irregular waves, mean circulation and nonlinear shallow-water evolution.

## Claims

- **C1281.** A descriptive overview identifies shoaling, refraction and diffraction as fundamental transformations as surface-gravity waves move from deep to shallow coastal water, with shoaling increasing height as propagation speed decreases. *Regime: Shoaling, Refraction and Diffraction in Waves.* [literature_review_statement, review] (Sakhaee 2025, [doi:10.37179/msdaeest.000010](https://doi.org/10.37179/msdaeest.000010))
